extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners, IP attorneys and patent applicants (particularly in ASEAN Member States / AMS)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing patentability (novelty and inventive step) including treatment of numerical ranges, second medical use claims, scope of prior art, tests for inventive step (problem-solution and Windsurfing), and definition of the person skilled in the art across AMS jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty of selected numerical sub-ranges (selection inventions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed invention may be novel by selecting a narrower sub-range of numerical values within a broader known range, provided the selected sub-range has not been explicitly mentioned in the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The selected sub-range should be narrow and sufficiently specific from the known broader range and ideally illustrated by examples. Whether a prior art reference anticipates a range depends on whether the claimed subject matter is disclosed with sufficient specificity in that prior art; interpretation of 'sufficient specificity' depends on the facts of the case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of overlap or touching borders on novelty of ranges
rubrics_metrics.description: If the numerical range disclosed in the prior-art document and the numerical range in the claimed subject matter are overlapping or at least share one border, the claimed subject matter does not involve novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Viet Nam guidance: overlapping ranges or even ranges 'close' to each other may destroy novelty; where two borders of the prior-art range are present and the claimed feature includes one of those borders (in contexts of discontinuous numbers), novelty is destroyed, whereas numbers strictly between the borders may remain novel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Close-but-non-overlapping ranges may be novel (criteria for 'close')
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art which teaches a value or range very close to, but not overlapping or touching, the claimed range does not anticipate the claimed range and the claim is novel (though inventive step must still be considered).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Viet Nam sets out three criteria for when a 'close' claimed numerical range still meets novelty: (a) the claimed numerical range is sufficiently far removed from any specific number disclosed; (b) the claimed range is narrow compared to the specific number disclosed; (c) the claimed range provides an effect that makes the claimed subject matter 'special' (e.g., unexpected effect).

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection invention and unexpected results as novelty/inventive step support
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a claim is directed to a narrow range and the prior art discloses only a broad range, the narrow selection may be novel if not merely one way of carrying out the prior teaching, especially when there is evidence (e.g., unexpected results) that the advantageous effect occurs only within the claimed narrow range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unexpected results may support novelty (selection invention) and may also render the claims unobvious (inventive step). Assessment depends on the specific facts and evidence showing the special effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable forms of second medical use claims (general rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Second medical use claims (new medical use of known substances) are treated differently across AMS; certain claim formats are acceptable to confer patentability for a new medical use even if the substance itself is known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical allowable formats in several AMS: 'Product X for use in the treatment of disease Y', Swiss-type claims (or equivalent), 'Use of compound X in the manufacture of a medicament for the treatment of disease Y'. A straightforward 'Use of substance X for the treatment of disease Y' may be regarded as a method of treatment and excluded in some AMS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional conditions for patenting second medical uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceptance of second medical use claims depends on jurisdictional requirements such as claim format, novelty of therapeutic application, and demonstration of new technical effect or enhanced efficacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Philippines accepts Swiss-type claims or Swiss-type-equivalents but requires the therapeutic application to be a truly new technical effect (different pathology) and demands enhanced efficacy for known compounds when claiming variants (salts, polymorphs, isomers, etc.). Thailand rejects Swiss-type claims and permits only manufacturing-use style claims that do not concern dosage, efficacy or application into a body. Indonesia's 2016 law excludes new uses not offering significant efficiency increase, though later guidelines may allow medical use claims in Swiss-type or specified formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'invention' for patentability purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'invention' is what is specified in the claim(s): commonly a solution to a technical problem that produces a technical effect; can be a product, process, or product-by-process; improvements of known products/processes can also be inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term 'improvement' does not necessarily require superior technical effect; the problem might be seeking an alternative providing the same or similar effects (e.g., cost-effectiveness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of inventive step (non-obviousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed invention involves an inventive step if, having regard to the prior art, it is not obvious (i.e., would not have been obvious) to a Person Skilled in the Art (PSIA) at the relevant date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventive step is generally equated with 'non-obvious' or 'not obvious'—meaning it goes beyond normal progress and does not 'follow plainly or logically' from prior art. Some AMS characterize it as 'inventive progress'. Guidance cites PCT/EPO formulations that the lack of inventive step is when something 'does not involve the exercise of any skill or ability beyond that to be expected of the PSIA.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and composition of prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: For assessing inventive step and novelty, prior art includes everything made available to the public anywhere in the world before the relevant date (filing or priority date).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This includes written disclosures, oral disclosures (public lectures), prior use/sale/display, internet disclosures, and is not limited by geography, language, or age. Unpublished patent applications with earlier priority are treated differently (to be disregarded for obviousness analysis in some contexts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Internet disclosures and assessment of publication dates
rubrics_metrics.description: Online disclosures are treated as written prior art as of the date they were publicly posted; websites and online databases can form prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners may accept online publication dates at face value absent indications to the contrary; online technical journals, reputable institutions, standard bodies are considered reliable. Where dates/content are unreliable or absent, examiners may seek further evidence; computer-generated timestamps and 'last modified' dates can be treated as publication dates unless contested. The applicant bears the burden to show otherwise if contesting dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit (inherent) disclosure as prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art disclosures may be implicit; teachings that are inherent in a prior art document count as part of the prior art and can destroy novelty or inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit teachings should be considered based on whether the implicit information is necessarily derivable from the prior-art disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental considerations when testing inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: Key considerations: (i) consider the claimed invention as a whole; (ii) consider prior arts as a whole; (iii) avoid impermissible hindsight when assessing obviousness; (iv) assess from the perspective of the PSIA with their general knowledge at the relevant date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For combination claims, it's not sufficient to show that separate features are known unless the claim is a mere aggregation without synergistic effect. Examiners should guard against ex post facto reasoning and attempt to visualise the real-life prior art confronting the PSIA before the invention was made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem-solution approach for assessing inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: A three-step method: (i) determine the closest prior art; (ii) establish the objective technical problem to be solved; (iii) consider whether the claimed invention, starting from the closest prior art and the objective technical problem, would have been obvious to the PSIA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Closest prior art is the single reference most promising as a starting point—preferably same field/use and having the most features in common. Objective technical problem is formulated by comparing claimed invention and closest prior art and may be reformulated based on objectively established facts and evidence in the proceedings. Partial or multiple technical problems (where distinguishing features yield different technical effects) should be handled part-by-part. The examiner must ask whether there was any teaching that would have 'prompted' the PSIA to modify the closest prior art to arrive at the claimed invention with a reasonable likelihood of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Windsurfing / Pozzoli four-step test for obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: A four-step test (Windsurfing, refined by Pozzoli): (i) identify the notional PSIA and their common general knowledge; (ii) identify/construe the inventive concept of the claim; (iii) identify differences between prior art and inventive concept; (iv) decide (without knowledge of the invention) whether those differences would have been obvious to the PSIA or require an inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach does not require identifying the single 'closest prior art' but focuses on whether the differences would have been obvious to the PSIA in view of common general knowledge and relevant prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and attributes of the Person Skilled in the Art (PSIA)
rubrics_metrics.description: The PSIA is a hypothetical person having common general knowledge in the relevant technical field and the ability to use ordinary technical means for R&D, exercise ordinary creativity in selecting materials, optimizing numerical ranges, and replacing elements with equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most AMS define the PSIA as having average or ordinary skill (setting a floor/ceiling for inventive step). The PSIA's knowledge includes field-specific common general knowledge; some self-evident scientific features need not be specified. The PSIA standard excludes persons of extraordinary skill.
